entities.name: Guy I of Luxembourg, Count of Ligny
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Guy I of Luxembourg-Ligny, born in 1340, was a significant figure in the intricate tapestry of Franco-English relations during the Hundred Years' War, serving as Count of Saint-Pol (1360–1371) and Count of Ligny (1364–1371). As a scion of the powerful Luxembourg dynasty, his strategic marriages and military service positioned him at the nexus of dynastic power struggles between the French Valois and English Plantagenets. His brief but impactful life, culminating in his death in 1371, was characterized by loyal service to the French crown, particularly under King Charles V, and by the establishment of a lineage that would profoundly influence the Burgundian State and later European royalty. He represented the shifting allegiances and territorial ambitions characteristic of 14th-century feudal Europe.

Guy I inherited the County of Saint-Pol from his mother, Jeanne, in 1360, consolidating his family's influence in Artois, a crucial border region. Four years later, he succeeded his father, Jean I, as Count of Ligny, further enhancing his territorial holdings and strategic importance. He actively participated in the ongoing conflicts of the Hundred Years' War, notably campaigning for King Charles V of France against the English and their allies. His military career saw him engaged in various skirmishes and sieges, contributing to the French efforts to regain territories lost after the Treaty of Brétigny, solidifying his reputation as a loyal and capable feudal lord.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Guy I was a significant regional figure whose strategic alliances and military service contributed to the French war effort during the Hundred Years' War. His most lasting impact was through his progeny, who played crucial roles in the powerful Burgundian State for generations, linking his lineage to major European political developments.
